Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
thehackernews.com · 23 Nov 2026 12:41 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSconnectwisecve-2026-84869huntressionosmanaged-service-providersmasterdarky-comremote-accesssckitscreenconnectscreenconnect-accesstelegram
96
In plain words

Criminals are using a serious flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, a tool that IT service providers use to remotely help customers, to take over the computers of support technicians without showing a warning. Once a technician connects to a session, an attacker can place and run a file that installs their own remote-control software. This puts managed service providers and their customers at risk because a technician’s computer may hold saved passwords and tools that can reach many customer systems. Updating ScreenConnect and checking affected technician computers can help limit the damage.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting the critical ConnectWise ScreenConnect flaw CVE-2026-84869 to silently push and execute malicious files on MSP technicians’ workstations, enabling remote takeover and access to customer environments. Organizations should update ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later and investigate potentially exposed technician systems.

Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-84869, a critical ConnectWise ScreenConnect client flaw rated 9.9, to target managed service provider (MSP) technician workstations. The flaw enables a guest in a remote session to send and run a malicious file on the connecting technician’s computer without a prompt appearing. Huntress observed one such compromise execute a guest-pushed batch file, contact a Telegram bot, download a fake Windows update installer, and launch a rogue ScreenConnect client in about nine seconds.

Huntress recorded at least 688,000 guest “run file” requests across 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses between October 20 and November 16, 2026. Attackers also used harmless marker files to check whether the technique worked before sending a payload, while another activity cluster registered thousands of fake guest sessions with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names. A compromised technician workstation is especially valuable because it can contain remote-management consoles, saved credentials, and access to many customer environments. Organizations are advised to update ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, investigate affected systems, and remove the TransferFiles permission if they cannot patch immediately.

  • The flaw can be triggered simply by a technician joining a remote session, with no warning or approval prompt shown before the malicious file is run on the technician’s computer.
  • Attackers used a harmless file named marker.txt seconds after a technician connected as a canary test, allowing them to verify that the technique worked before delivering a harmful payload.
  • Some attackers created fake ScreenConnect guest sessions with cryptocurrency exchange-themed computer names to entice technicians to connect, even when no later file transfer or command activity was observed.
  • Because technician workstations may contain remote-management tools and saved credentials for many customers, compromising one technician can provide access well beyond a single affected computer.
  • If organizations cannot immediately update ScreenConnect, removing the TransferFiles permission from relevant roles and session groups is a documented interim mitigation.
Key Points
  • 01Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-84869, a critical ConnectWise ScreenConnect client flaw with a CVSS score of 9.9, to transfer and execute files on a connecting technician’s host.
  • 02Huntress observed an MSP technician workstation run a guest-pushed batch file that contacted a Telegram bot, downloaded a Windows-update-themed MSI installer, and launched a rogue ScreenConnect client within about nine seconds.
  • 03Between October 20 and November 16, 2026, Huntress recorded at least 688,000 guest “run file” requests targeting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses.
  • 04Huntress also identified 2,408 unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions across at least 118 self-hosted servers belonging to 109 protected organizations, with many using cryptocurrency exchange-themed names.
  • 05Organizations are advised to update technician ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, or remove the TransferFiles permission if patching cannot occur immediately.

JUSTIFICATION

This is an active exploitation report involving a critical CVSS 9.9 ConnectWise ScreenConnect flaw that can silently compromise MSP technician workstations. The potential impact is high because compromised technician systems may provide access to remote-management tools, saved credentials, and numerous customer environments.

In plain words

The U.S. cyber agency CISA says criminals are actively taking advantage of a serious weakness in Cisco Expressway systems, which organizations use to connect internal voice and video services with people outside the organization. The flaw can let an outsider take full control of affected internet-connected systems and then move into other parts of an organization’s network. U.S. federal agencies have been ordered to fix it within three days, and CISA is urging private organizations to do the same because attackers may use it to steal sensitive information or spread further through their systems.

Summary
CISA has added Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attackers used it to gain root-level remote command execution on exposed devices. Organizations should urgently patch affected Expressway-C and Expressway-E cluster deployments.

CISA has added CVE-2026-76466, a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog after identifying it as actively exploited. The agency ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure affected systems within three days under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. CISA also urged private-sector defenders to prioritize patching because the flaw poses significant risks to networks.

The vulnerability affects clustered Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices and stems from hard-coded credentials and incomplete validation of client certificates. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute operating-system commands as root. F6 reported attackers compromised two internet-facing Expressway devices, used one to access two internal cluster nodes, and prepared Python tooling to scan networks, access SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and inspect GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information.

  • An internet-facing Cisco Expressway device can provide a path to additional cluster nodes on an organization’s internal network, as F6 observed attackers moving from two exposed devices to two internal nodes.
  • The reported post-compromise tooling was designed to locate SMB shares, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and examine GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information.
  • CISA designated the issue as actively exploited even though Cisco said its incident-response team was not aware of in-the-wild exploitation or public proof-of-concept code when patches were released.
  • F6 reported that the attackers used an unnamed AI assistant while exploiting the Cisco Expressway flaw and obtaining root-level access.
Key Points
  • 01CISA added CVE-2026-76466, a critical Cisco Expressway flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog after identifying it as actively exploited.
  • 02The flaw affects clustered Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices and can allow unauthenticated attackers to run operating-system commands as root because of hard-coded credentials and incomplete client-certificate validation.
  • 03CISA ordered U.S. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure affected systems within three days under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.
  • 04F6 reported that attackers compromised two internet-facing Cisco Expressway devices, reached two additional internal cluster nodes, and prepared tools for further movement across the network.
  • 05Cisco said in late October that it released patches for the issue, while its PSIRT was not aware of active exploitation or public proof-of-concept code at that time.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a critical, actively exploited remote-code-execution vulnerability that can give unauthenticated attackers root-level control of affected Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E cluster deployments. CISA added CVE-2026-76466 to KEV and directed federal agencies to remediate it within three days, while reported intrusions included movement from exposed devices into internal cluster nodes.

    In plain words

    Hackers used a security weakness in an older Microsoft cloud service to try to obtain passwords and other sensitive access information from Norwegian energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. The companies said their oil, gas, and electricity operations continued normally and found no sign that information was stolen, but Equinor’s internal services were disrupted. Norwegian authorities say organizations in multiple sectors and countries may be affected, and warn that more criminals could try to use the flaw now that it is public.

    Summary
    Norwegian authorities say attackers exploited a flaw in legacy Azure API Management tiers to target sensitive credentials at energy firms Equinor and Skagerak Energi. Microsoft fixed the exposure path and urged affected customers to rotate credentials, while the companies reported no confirmed data theft or operational disruption.

    Norway’s National Security Authority said an unidentified threat actor exploited a security flaw in Microsoft Azure API Management to target access tokens and other sensitive information. Norwegian energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi reported cyberattacks last week, and authorities said organizations across multiple sectors in Norway and abroad could be affected. Equinor helped identify the issue and alert authorities.

    Equinor detected its incident on Tuesday and contained it by Friday, reporting disruption to some internal services but no effect on oil and gas production and no indication that data was stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi said its operations and electricity production were unaffected and that it found no evidence of compromised information. Microsoft said the issue affected older Azure API Management tiers, particularly where customers stored sensitive information directly in the service rather than Azure Key Vault or had not followed security recommendations; it closed the access path, notified potentially affected customers, and published guidance to rotate credentials.

    • The exposure primarily concerned customers that stored sensitive information directly in Azure API Management or had not followed Microsoft’s security recommendations, rather than all Azure API Management users.
    • Newer Azure API Management versions were not affected, while Microsoft said several older tiers—including Developer, Basic, Standard, and Premium—were impacted.
    • Equinor helped identify the issue and alert Norwegian authorities, meaning the vulnerability was first discovered through Norway’s energy sector.
    • Microsoft had closed the identified access path before publicly publishing credential-rotation guidance, but did not disclose how many customers may have been exposed.
    • Norwegian authorities said they had found no evidence that successful or attempted compromises disrupted services at Norwegian organizations, despite the incidents involving energy companies.
    Key Points
    • 01Norway’s National Security Authority said an unidentified threat actor actively targeted access tokens and other sensitive information through a flaw in Azure API Management.
    • 02Equinor and Skagerak Energi reported cyberattacks, but both said their core energy production continued normally and neither found evidence that information had been compromised.
    • 03Equinor detected the incident on Tuesday and fully contained it by Friday, with some internal services disrupted.
    • 04Microsoft said it discovered the issue affecting older Classic Azure API Management tiers on November 18 and closed the access path the next day.
    • 05Microsoft advised potentially affected customers to identify and rotate exposed credentials, while Norwegian authorities warned that organizations in multiple sectors in Norway and abroad could be affected.

In plain words

Microsoft found and fixed a weakness in an older version of its Azure API Management service that may have let outsiders retrieve customers’ stored passwords, access keys, and other digital credentials. Organizations using that older service, including companies in Norway’s energy sector, may be affected; Equinor and Skagerak Energi reported attempted or ongoing cyberattacks. The risk is serious because stolen credentials can open the door to other company applications, services, and internal systems, so customers need to replace exposed credentials and check for suspicious activity.

Summary
Microsoft mitigated an exploited flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers that could let unauthorized actors access stored secrets, subscription keys, and management tokens. Affected customers must rotate potentially exposed credentials and investigate for misuse, as the fix does not invalidate credentials stolen before mitigation.

Microsoft warned that an exploited vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers could have allowed unauthorized parties to access stored customer credentials. The company said it identified the issue on November 18, 2026, and closed the unauthorized management-access path the following day. Potentially exposed information included secrets in Named Values, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys, and tokens for direct management APIs.

Microsoft rotated Microsoft-controlled keys where appropriate, but said its fix does not automatically invalidate customer credentials that may have been accessed before mitigation. It urged affected organizations to rotate potentially exposed credentials, examine logs, and investigate suspicious activity in connected systems. Norway’s National Security Authority linked the issue to attacks involving Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, and advised customers to confirm their APIM instances had received the security update.

  • Microsoft’s fix blocked the unauthorized access route but did not revoke customer credentials that may already have been copied, making credential rotation a separate and urgent customer responsibility.
  • The potentially exposed data included credentials that could grant access beyond API Management itself, such as to connected applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions.
  • Norway’s National Security Authority advised organizations to confirm that their individual API Management instances received the update, noting that instances below certain runtime versions remain vulnerable.
  • A Reddit administrator alleged that the legacy API involved did not produce customer-visible logs for the unauthorized access, but BleepingComputer said it had not independently verified that claim.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft said an exploited flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers allowed unauthorized access to management functions and potentially exposed stored secrets, subscription keys, and management API tokens.
  • 02Microsoft identified the issue on November 18, 2026, closed the unauthorized access path on November 19, and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate.
  • 03Microsoft warned that its remediation does not automatically invalidate customer credentials that may have been accessed before the fix, and urged affected customers to rotate credentials and investigate suspicious activity.
  • 04Norway’s National Security Authority linked the issue to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, and said organizations in other countries and industries were also affected.
  • 05Microsoft said Azure API Management v2 tiers are not affected, while Norway’s National Security Authority advised organizations to verify that their API Management instances received the security update.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an actively exploited Azure API Management Classic vulnerability that may have exposed secrets, subscription keys, and management tokens, with reported impact on Norwegian energy organizations. Microsoft’s mitigation does not invalidate credentials potentially stolen before the fix, making immediate credential rotation and investigation important for affected customers.

Hackers Exploit Critical ASP.NET Anti-CSRF Library Flaw Allowing Unauthenticated RCE
thehackernews.com · 23 Nov 2026 09:11 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSasp-net-webformscve-2026-131914google-cloudgoogle-mandiantidunnoidunno-anticrsfiismicrosoftobjectstateformatter-deserialization
94
In plain words

Researchers found that criminals are actively abusing a serious flaw in an old, unsupported software add-on used to protect some ASP.NET web applications from unwanted form submissions. Any organization still using the Idunno.AntiCsrf add-on could let an outsider take control of its web server with a single specially made request, without needing to log in. This could expose the application, its stored passwords and keys, and other systems connected to that server, so affected organizations should stop using the add-on and check for signs of intrusion.

Summary
A critical, actively exploited insecure-deserialization flaw in the obsolete Idunno.AntiCsrf ASP.NET library lets unauthenticated attackers execute code on vulnerable IIS web servers with a single crafted POST request. Organizations should immediately remove or replace the unsupported library and investigate affected systems for compromise.

Google Mandiant has warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-131914, a critical flaw in the discontinued Idunno.AntiCsrf library for ASP.NET WebForms. The vulnerability affects versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta and has a CVSS score of 9.3. Idunno.AntiCsrf has not been updated since December 2008, and no official patch is available.

The flaw occurs because the library processes untrusted anti-CSRF form-token data without cryptographic verification when handling HTTP POST requests. An unauthenticated attacker can send a single crafted request, using any non-empty configured anti-CSRF cookie value and a specially encoded form value, to execute arbitrary code as the IIS worker process. Organizations are advised to remove the library, replace it with a supported alternative, review IIS logs for suspicious POST activity, and rotate relevant configuration secrets if exploitation is suspected.

  • A component intended to protect ASP.NET WebForms applications from cross-site request forgery can instead be used to run arbitrary code because it processes attacker-supplied form-token data without cryptographic verification.
  • Exploitation does not require an account or a valid anti-CSRF token; according to Mandiant, an attacker only needs to send a POST request containing any non-empty configured CSRF cookie value and a specially encoded form-field value.
  • The article identifies practical hunting signals: anomalous POST requests to .aspx pages that return HTTP 302 or HTTP 500 responses and have unusually high request-byte counts where IIS logging captures them.
  • Because successful exploitation can compromise the IIS worker process, organizations with evidence of compromise are advised to rotate Web.config and applicationHost.config secrets, including machine keys, encryption keys, and database credentials, and inspect webroots for unauthorized files.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-131914 is a critical insecure-deserialization flaw in Idunno.AntiCsrf versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta, with a CVSS score of 9.3.
  • 02The flaw can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code in the IIS worker process through a single crafted HTTP POST request to affected ASP.NET WebForms endpoints.
  • 03Google Mandiant reported that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild.
  • 04Idunno.AntiCsrf has not been updated since December 2008, and no official patch is available.
  • 05Organizations are advised to discontinue Idunno.AntiCsrf, adopt a supported anti-CSRF alternative, review IIS logs for suspicious POST requests, and rotate relevant secrets if compromise is suspected.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is an actively exploited critical vulnerability that enables unauthenticated remote code execution through a single crafted POST request. Organizations still using the unsupported Idunno.AntiCsrf library face potential complete compromise of affected IIS-hosted ASP.NET WebForms servers and have no vendor patch to apply.

In plain words

South Korea’s main electricity company, KEPCO, says someone broke into two of its internal systems and viewed information belonging to more than 1.5 million people. The exposed records include customer contact and billing details, and in some cases bank account or payment-card information, as well as employee and contractor information. This could let criminals create convincing scams or pretend to be KEPCO, so affected people should be cautious about unexpected calls, texts, links, requests for information, or verification codes.

Summary
South Korea’s state-controlled power utility KEPCO confirmed that attackers accessed its billing and procurement systems, exposing personal and financial data belonging to more than 1.5 million customers, representatives, and employees. The company has restricted access, notified affected people, and is coordinating with authorities to prevent fraud.

Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), South Korea’s state-controlled main electric power company, confirmed that an unauthorized party accessed two internal systems: the KEPCO ON electricity billing platform and the SRM electronic procurement system. KEPCO detected the incident on November 20 and said it blocked external IP access and suspended the affected services. The company said it is notifying affected individuals, reported the incident to data-protection authorities, and is working with government and financial authorities to prevent unauthorized transactions.

The exposure affected more than 1.5 million people, including 650,487 KEPCO ON customers, 426,827 company representatives, and 442,934 KEPCO employees. Customer records included names, identification and contact details, addresses, electricity billing information, and, in some cases, bank-account or payment-card information; employee and representative records also included personal and business contact details. KEPCO warned that the information could support targeted phishing and impersonation, while a person using the alias Noiem claimed responsibility for the incident, though attribution remains unconfirmed.

  • The combination of customer contact information, billing details, and in some cases bank or card data creates a strong basis for highly convincing scams that impersonate KEPCO.
  • The incident affected both public-facing billing services and a procurement system, exposing not only customers but also company representatives, employees, and contractor-related records.
  • KEPCO attributed the breach generally to “advanced technologies such as AI” but did not disclose how the intruder initially gained access or moved through its systems.
  • Although Noiem publicly claimed the breach before KEPCO’s announcement, the article states that the claimed attribution has not been confirmed.

13 Malicious NuGet Packages Target .NET Developers With Fake Job Assessments

TAGSchrome-profile-stealerclickfixcontagious-interviewdll-side-loadinggithubgithub-c2happyone-msbuildanalyzeriranmicrosoftmsbuild-executionnorth-koreanugetvs-builder-msbuildanalyzerweapfwinui-button

In plain words

Researchers found 13 harmful software add-ons for .NET developers, along with fake coding tests and a fake crypto-wallet project designed to trick job seekers into running them on Windows computers. Some of these add-ons quietly downloaded and started other programs, while others used legitimate Windows files to load harmful code. This puts developers, their saved browser passwords and login sessions, and the organizations whose code and cloud accounts they can access at risk. The case shows that a job assignment or seemingly simple interface component can be a route into a person’s computer and workplace systems.

Summary
Socket identified a coordinated campaign using 13 malicious NuGet packages and fake .NET job assessments to infect Windows developers through MSBuild build hooks, DLL side-loading, and button controls that download and execute payloads. Developers should treat take-home projects and bundled NuGet packages as untrusted, particularly packages containing build targets or unfamiliar UI controls.

Socket’s Threat Research Team identified an operation involving 13 malicious NuGet packages, fake .NET job assessments, GitHub-hosted payloads, and a trojanized crypto-wallet application targeting Windows developers. Most packages impersonated WinUI 3 or WPF button controls, while the lures instructed candidates to build and run Visual Studio projects on native Windows. The operation also included malicious npm packages, executable files disguised as .csproj project files, GitHub-based command-and-control, and a ClickFix page that copied a hidden PowerShell command.

One fake WinUI 3 assessment bundled NuGet packages that caused MSBuild to run a DLL after every build, downloading OskSupport.dll into %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\ and copying Windows osk.exe beside it. Its FileButton control then launched the copied osk.exe when the application created the control, using a known DLL side-loading arrangement. Separately, WinUI.Button started a background downloader from its button constructor that retrieved an executable from GitHub, saved it as %TEMP%\Launcher.exe, and ran it. The recovered payloads included loaders that used private GitHub repositories for per-victim instructions, a Chrome-profile stealer that uploaded collected data to GitHub, and a payload that reported information through Telegram.

The article warns that developers can be exposed simply by building or running a take-home project or adding an apparently harmless interface-control package. It recommends treating coding assessments as untrusted, reviewing local package feeds and bundled .nupkg files, and using disposable virtual machines with no access to credentials for untrusted projects. Organizations are advised to restrict NuGet package sources and review packages containing build targets that execute commands, while security teams are advised to hunt for indicators including %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\, %TEMP%\Launcher.exe, suspicious MSBuild-launched dotnet.exe processes, and unusual authenticated GitHub API activity.

  • The fake assessment used two separate components that only complete the infection chain together: one prepares files during a build, and the other launches the copied Windows program when the app window creates its button control.
  • The MSBuild target declares an output file that is never created, causing the malicious DLL to run after every build rather than being treated as already complete.
  • After NuGet removed the original packages, the lure initially carried malicious .nupkg files inside its own repository and configured the project to restore packages from that local folder.
  • The malicious WinUI.Button package does not need a user to click anything: merely creating its WUIButton control starts a background task that repeatedly tries to download and run an executable.
  • The recovered loader uses private GitHub repository paths as a per-victim command channel, allowing operators to receive a machine profile and place a distinct next-stage payload for each victim.
Key Points
  • 01Socket identified 13 malicious NuGet packages targeting Windows .NET developers through fake job-related “Home Assessment” projects and deceptive WinUI 3 or WPF button controls.
  • 02A bundled MSBuild target in the fake WinUI 3 assessment runs after every build and downloads a DLL to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll while copying Windows On-Screen Keyboard, osk.exe, beside it.
  • 03The assessment’s FileButton control launches the copied osk.exe when the application creates the control, using a known DLL side-loading arrangement involving osksupport.dll.
  • 04WinUI.Button 1.0.0 starts a background downloader from its WUIButton constructor that retrieves avast.exe from GitHub, saves it as %TEMP%\Launcher.exe, and runs it.
  • 05The operation also used GitHub-hosted executables disguised as axios.csproj files, a trojanized Crypto Wallet Analyzer application, GitHub repositories for command-and-control, and a ClickFix page that copies a PowerShell command.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a detailed report on an active, concrete supply-chain operation targeting Windows .NET developers through malicious NuGet packages, fake job assessments, and GitHub-hosted payload infrastructure. It includes a still-installable package, build-time code execution, runtime downloaders, actionable indicators, hashes, and detection guidance relevant to developer-security and incident-response teams.

In plain words

Hackers used a weakness in GL.iNet’s online device-management service to place harmful software on some of the company’s travel routers and remote-control devices. People who own these devices may have had outsiders gain full control of them, and computers connected through the remote-control devices could also be at risk. Summary
Attackers exploited a flaw in GL.iNet’s GoodCloud remote-management service to run root-level malware on some routers and KVM devices; GL.iNet has blocked the access path and released security firmware. Owners should check for compromise, update immediately, and consider reinstalling firmware without retaining settings and rotating stored credentials if infection is suspected.

Attackers exploited a flaw in GL.iNet’s GoodCloud remote-management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM remote-control devices. GL.iNet said it fixed the cloud-side issue and blocked the access route used by the attacker, but that change does not remove malware from devices already affected. The company released security firmware for listed router and KVM models and is contacting customers it identifies as affected, though it has not disclosed the number of infections, the attacker’s identity, or how GoodCloud was breached.

RemoteToHome Consulting verified a root-level remote command shell on a managed GL-AXT1800 router with GoodCloud enabled, while other managed devices showed related activity. Its analysis says a GoodCloud client handler accepted two values from cloud messages and ran them as root without validation, although GL.iNet has not confirmed that technical finding. The observed shell left no files and disappeared after a restart, and the vendor’s published process marker was absent on the router with the verified shell.

GL.iNet says the listed firmware updates remove malware from this incident without requiring a factory reset and retain device settings. Researchers caution that retaining settings may preserve password files, SSH keys, user directories, and potentially boot-time scripts on KVM devices, and recommend reinstalling firmware without keeping settings if compromise is suspected. They also advise treating saved credentials and keys as exposed, while disabling GoodCloud can stop the cloud client until an update is installed but will not clean an already infected device.

  • The vendor’s suggested process marker can miss infections: RemoteToHome found it absent on a router where it verified a root-level reverse shell.
  • The observed router shell leaves no files behind and its traces disappear after a restart, so checking a suspected device before rebooting or upgrading can preserve evidence.
  • Researchers found that an earlier KVM security upgrade retained password files, SSH keys, and user directories containing boot-time scripts, so they recommend reinstalling firmware without keeping settings when compromise is suspected.
  • Turning off GoodCloud stops the cloud client from running until an update is installed, but it does not remove malware already placed on a device.
  • RemoteToHome also found an older, unrelated backdoor on 49 managed routers that was installed between September 2025 and May 2026, with no established link to the GoodCloud incident.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet’s GoodCloud remote-management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices.
  • 02GL.iNet said it fixed the cloud-side flaw and blocked the attacker’s access route, but devices infected before the fix still require checking and installation of the listed security firmware.

  • 04GL.iNet’s updated security notice says its listed firmware versions remove the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset, while researchers recommend reinstalling firmware without retaining settings when compromise is suspected.
  • 05The number of affected devices, the attacker’s identity, and the method used to breach the GoodCloud service remain unknown.

N-able disclosed and fixed CVE-2026-134624, a critical server-side request forgery issue in its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud email-filtering service. The issue was discovered while the company investigated unauthorized access to one Hosted Cloud server. N-able restored dashboard and API access late Saturday after an outage that began the previous Monday, while email delivery and spam filtering continued operating. The company has not said whether the flaw was used to gain access.

The flaw was in an LDAP synchronization connection check used when a relay is configured. A user with high-level API access could direct the server to connect to chosen internal hosts and ports, determine which were reachable, and send crafted data to internal services; N-able assigned it a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3 and fixed it in build 20261121.1943. During its response, the company took the affected server offline, rotated internal credentials, revoked customer API and OAuth tokens, and reset local user passwords. N-able says it has found no evidence of compromised customer data or activity beyond the affected server, but customers must replace revoked credentials used by scripts and integrations.

  • SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware and is covered by weekly software updates, so its operators should verify that they are running build 20261121.1943.
  • N-able has not determined or disclosed how the unauthorized party initially accessed the Hosted Cloud server, and says a formal root-cause analysis is expected within two weeks of its update.

In plain words

Researchers sent about two million test messages containing unique secret links through popular AI services and found that attackers and some service providers could access them, even when the services promised not to keep the data. Companies using AI tools, especially automated AI helpers, may unknowingly send passwords, customer information, code, or private documents through several outside companies before reaching the AI model. This matters because a promise not to save data may not protect it if another company in the chain is compromised or reads the request, leaving organizations unable to know exactly what was exposed.

Summary
Dragos researchers found that AI prompts sent through hosting providers and marketplaces—including requests marked zero data retention—were exposed through provider breaches, reseller logging, and undisclosed routing. Organizations should treat prompts as sensitive outbound data, restrict AI routing, scan agent inputs for secrets, and maintain records of what agents send.

Dragos researchers placed unique, trackable secrets in about 2 million prompts sent through widely used AI services and reported three major findings: breaches at three hosting providers, prompt exposure through marketplace resellers, and failures of zero-data-retention (ZDR) settings. In the largest breach, attackers captured requests at a provider’s entry point, obtained hundreds of AWS keys, and used them for tens of thousands of AWS API calls. The researchers said some intercepted requests had been rejected before reaching a model, showing that prompts could be copied before inference occurred.

The article argues that AI prompts should be treated as sensitive data leaving an organization because they may contain source code, customer records, contracts, and credentials. It notes that routing services can send a request through multiple providers, each of which may see the full prompt and response under separate policies, while ZDR promises may apply only to the first hop. The article recommends inventorying AI tools and routes, restricting providers for sensitive work, checking prompts and agent tool outputs for secrets, placing canary credentials in agent context, and retaining records of what agents send so exposed data and credentials can be identified after an incident.

  • A request can be exposed even if no AI model processes it, because the largest reported breach captured prompts at a hosting provider’s entry point, including requests the provider rejected.
  • A zero-data-retention setting is not an end-to-end guarantee: the article states that it binds only the first service receiving the request, while routers and downstream providers may handle the full prompt and response under separate policies.
  • Automated AI agents can leak secrets without a user knowingly entering them, because configuration files, database results, and other tool outputs can be added to later AI requests automatically.
  • When an AI provider discloses an incident, organizations may be unable to determine which credentials to rotate unless they have retained records of the prompts, tool calls, and results their agents sent.
Key Points
  • 01Dragos researchers placed unique trackable secrets in about 2 million prompts sent to widely used AI services and reported that attackers accessed three AI hosting providers for up to four months.
  • 02In the largest reported provider breach, attackers captured requests at the provider entry point, obtained hundreds of AWS keys, and made tens of thousands of AWS API calls against the canary keys.
  • 03Dragos found that marketplace resellers could log customer prompts, and individuals on home internet connections opened secret URLs and manually tried associated passwords.
  • 04One Chinese AI lab opened secret links in roughly two-thirds of requests marked zero data retention or no data collection, despite those settings stating that prompts and responses would not be stored.
  • 05The article recommends that organizations inventory their AI providers and routing paths, restrict sensitive-work routing, inspect prompts and tool results for credentials, use canary credentials, and retain records of agent activity.

In plain words

A serious flaw was found in binary-parser, a widely used software component for handling binary data in JavaScript applications. If someone can control the instructions used to set up a parser, they may be able to make the application run their own code when that parser is prepared. This affects versions older than 2.3.1, while programs that only process untrusted data using trusted parser instructions are not affected. Updating to the latest version helps prevent outsiders from taking control of the affected application process.

Summary
Binary-parser versions before 2.3.1 have a critical code-injection flaw (CVE-2026-134814) that can let attackers who control parser definitions execute arbitrary JavaScript in Node.js during parser compilation. Users should upgrade to version 2.3.1 or later.

A critical code-injection flaw, CVE-2026-134814, affects binary-parser versions before 2.3.1. The issue can allow attackers who control parser definitions to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when a parser is compiled. The vulnerability has been assigned CVSS scores of 9.2 and 8.1.

The problem arose because certain user-controlled string options were inserted into generated JavaScript without sufficient validation. Affected options include length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, and aliases supplied through namely(). Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected, according to the maintainer. Version 2.3.1 validates these values as identifier paths and rejects expressions such as “len - 1,” while CVE-2026-134814 is also described as an incomplete fix for the earlier CVE-2026-1245.

  • The risk depends on who controls the parser definition: processing untrusted binary data alone is not affected when the parser definition is trusted.
  • The patch deliberately disallows expression-style option values such as "len - 1" and requires a function instead, which may require application changes beyond simply updating the package.
  • The issue was identified as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245, showing that earlier validation improvements did not cover all user-controlled parser options.
  • The malicious code executes when the parser is compiled, meaning the dangerous input is the parser setup information rather than the binary data being parsed.
Key Points
  • 01Binary-parser versions before 2.3.1 contain CVE-2026-134814, a code-injection flaw that can allow arbitrary JavaScript execution when an attacker controls parser definitions.
  • 02The flaw stems from string options such as length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, and aliases passed to namely() being inserted into generated JavaScript without adequate validation.
  • 03The vulnerability is triggered when a crafted parser definition is compiled in a Node.js process, not simply by parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition.
  • 04The binary-parser maintainer stated that version 2.3.1 validates these options as identifier paths and rejects expressions such as "len - 1."
  • 05CVE-2026-134814 is described as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245, an earlier code-injection issue involving insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.

In plain words

India’s cyber emergency agency says criminals are using artificial intelligence tools to break into banks, financial firms, and related service providers, then misuse normal payment approval steps to send money without permission. These incidents have led to large unauthorized transfers, often routed through accounts controlled by criminals and quickly moved elsewhere. The concern is that AI can help attackers work faster, adapt when blocked, and carry out many parts of an intrusion at once, putting organizations and their customers at greater financial risk.

Summary
CERT-In warns that AI-assisted attackers are abusing legitimate business workflows, records, and approval processes to trigger unauthorized payments at Indian banks, fintechs, and government-linked service providers. Agentic offensive tools are accelerating reconnaissance, exploitation, and lateral movement, shrinking financially motivated intrusions from days to hours.

CERT-In warned that AI-assisted attackers are targeting Indian information and communication technology assets, causing unauthorized financial transactions at banks, financial services firms, technology providers, and government-linked payment platforms. The agency said attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used otherwise legitimate payment processes rather than directly exploiting payment APIs. It did not identify the actors involved or disclose the amount improperly paid out.

The Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre said campaigns against banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintechs led to multi-crore unauthorized transactions through fund-disbursement systems and payment-transfer interfaces. It said attackers compromise unpatched or misconfigured internet-facing systems, move funds into mule accounts, and quickly transfer or withdraw the money through IMPS and NEFT. CERT-In advised organizations to review the security of business applications, critical records, identities, and third-party interfaces, and to account for abuse of trusted processes in monitoring and incident response.

CERT-In also reported that agentic offensive frameworks can automate reconnaissance, create and modify exploits, conduct intrusion tasks in parallel, and adapt when blocked. In financially motivated Indian campaigns, the agency said such tooling compressed the period from initial access to final impact from days to a few hours. In plain words

Researchers say the China-aligned Webworm group may be using a modified version of legitimate remote-connection software to quietly maintain access to networks it has already entered. The group has targeted government bodies, IT service providers, and electric power companies in Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and other Asian countries. The altered software is made to look like ordinary network-monitoring software and normal web traffic, making it harder for security tools to spot. This matters because attackers can hide their access without needing to add obvious new malicious features.

Summary
China-aligned Webworm is suspected of rebuilding SoftEther VPN Bridge as a stealthy “NtMonitor VPN” remote-access tool, changing recognizable endpoints, protocol markers, and configuration storage to evade security detections.

Rapid7 assessed with moderate confidence that the China-aligned Webworm threat actor is using a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge to maintain concealed remote access to compromised networks. The Windows executable, netcapa.exe, is based on SoftEther VPN Bridge version 4.44 build 9807 and is rebranded as “NtMonitor VPN,” presented as network-monitoring software. Webworm has previously targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies in Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and other Asian countries.

The modified build changes recognizable SoftEther network endpoints to /update/alive.cgi and /update/picture.cgi so its activity resembles ordinary web application traffic. It also replaces SoftEther’s GIF-based connection marker with a PNG-based marker, minimizes and embeds a required resource archive, and encrypts a renamed configuration file, setting.conf, with a custom algorithm. Rapid7 found no new functionality added to the tool, indicating that the changes are intended primarily to reduce detection opportunities. Although the program disguises its external behavior, its included debugging path and some registry references still identify SoftEther components.

  • The altered tool adds no identified new functionality; its changes are focused on removing or changing recognizable signs that defenders could use to detect SoftEther VPN Bridge.
  • Although the software is disguised externally, its included PDB path still identifies it as SoftEther VPN Bridge, meaning the concealment is aimed at security tooling and network observation rather than reverse engineers.
  • The rebranding is incomplete because some Windows registry paths continue to refer to “SoftEther Project,” even where other references were changed to “NtMonitor VPN.”
  • The required SoftEther resource archive was reduced to a minimal version and embedded into the executable, increasing the binary size by about 1.5 MB while avoiding a separate runtime file.
Key Points
  • 01Rapid7 assessed with moderate confidence that the China-aligned Webworm group is using a custom build of SoftEther VPN Bridge to create covert remote access to compromised networks.
  • 02The Windows executable netcapa.exe is a modified SoftEther VPN Bridge version 4.44 build 9807 that is rebranded as “NtMonitor VPN” and presented as network-monitoring software.
  • 03The modified tool replaces SoftEther’s usual HTTP paths with /update/alive.cgi and /update/picture.cgi, making its communications resemble ordinary web application activity.
  • 04It replaces SoftEther’s GIF-based connection marker with a PNG-based marker, a change intended to bypass detections based on the original GIF marker.
  • 05The build encrypts its configuration file, renamed from vpn_bridge.config to setting.conf, with a custom algorithm and uses the ASCII magic bytes RCEN.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete, recent finding involving the China-aligned Webworm group modifying a legitimate remote-access tool to evade common detections. It is particularly relevant to defenders because it identifies specific behavioral and technical changes that can reduce the usefulness of existing SoftEther detection signatures.

In plain words

A scam email was sent to the accounts team at a small UK IT consultancy, pretending to be a short payment request from the firm’s own principal and including a fake supplier invoice. Although the email passed normal sender checks, hidden message details showed it was part of a bulk campaign, while the invoice used suspicious free email addresses and inconsistent billing details. This matters because a convincing request can trick staff into sending tens of thousands of pounds to criminals unless payment requests are confirmed through a known, separate way of contacting the requester.

Summary
A BEC invoice scam impersonated a UK consultancy’s principal and passed email authentication, but bulk-campaign headers, mismatched invoice details, and free-mail reply/remittance addresses exposed it as fraudulent. The key lesson is that DKIM, SPF, and DMARC validate the sending route—not the true author or legitimacy of a payment request.

A shared Accounts mailbox at a small UK IT and cloud-security consultancy received a one-line payment instruction impersonating the firm’s principal. The message included an HTML supplier invoice requesting payment of GBP 38,560.00 and claimed that a lapsed 30% discount would still be honored. A human analyst confirmed the email was malicious, and it was removed from the mailbox. The article describes it as business email compromise invoice fraud and executive impersonation.

Although the email appeared to be a personal executive request, its headers included a campaign List-ID, Precedence: bulk, an X-Entity-ID, and a complaints address. The timestamp embedded in the List-ID was three minutes earlier than the DKIM signing time, and DKIM covered both the List-ID and the free-mail Reply-To address, indicating those elements were present when the message was signed. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passed, but the article notes that these checks validated the delivery route rather than the person who wrote the email.

The invoice was billed to the same principal whose name appeared on the payment instruction, creating a misleading appearance of authorization. Its subject described an advisory engagement while the line items described platform licensing and implementation support; it also listed zero-rated reverse-charge VAT between a London supplier and a UK recipient, plus free-mail addresses for replies and remittance. The article recommends independently verifying payment requests through a known channel, especially when an executive-style note has bulk-mail headers or an invoice contains inconsistent details.

  • A supposedly personal executive payment request can be identified as suspicious when it carries bulk-mail headers such as List-ID and Precedence: bulk, because those headers are not expected in a one-to-one internal-style note.
  • The signed List-ID timestamp predating the email signature by three minutes shows the campaign marker was already part of the message when it was signed, rather than being added later in transit.
  • An invoice addressed to the same executive who is requesting payment creates a false sense of internal validation, so staff should verify it through a known channel rather than replying to the email.
  • Passing sender-authentication checks does not establish who authored a message; in this case, the message passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication while still being malicious.
  • Inconsistencies between an invoice subject, line items, VAT treatment, and free-mail remittance addresses provide practical warning signs even when the invoice arithmetic is correct.
Key Points
  • 01A one-line payment instruction impersonating a UK IT consultancy’s principal was sent to the firm’s shared Accounts mailbox with an invoice requesting GBP 38,560.00.
  • 02The email contained List-ID, Precedence: bulk, X-Entity-ID, and complaint-address headers associated with bulk mail, despite presenting itself as a personal executive request.
  • 03The List-ID timestamp was 10:06:13 UTC on 12 November 2026, three minutes before the DKIM signing time, and DKIM covered the List-ID and Reply-To headers.
  • 04SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication all passed, confirming the delivery route but not the identity of the person who wrote the payment request.
  • 05A human analyst confirmed the email was malicious and it was removed from the mailbox.

These scams reach people through fake emails, ads, websites, and even messages offering huge discounts, prizes, game bundles, beauty products, or subscriptions. Anyone shopping online can lose account passwords, card details, personal information, or money, while fake offers can also lead people to download harmful files. The article’s main warning is that busy holiday sales periods give scammers more opportunities to exploit trust in well-known brands and pressure people into acting quickly.

Summary
Kaspersky reports a sharp rise in shopping-related phishing and Black Friday spam in 2026, with scammers heavily impersonating Amazon, Apple, Netflix and other trusted brands to steal credentials, payment data and money. Shoppers should treat urgent, unusually cheap offers and unsolicited links with skepticism and verify retailers directly before entering personal or payment information.

Kaspersky’s 2026 Black Friday analysis found that phishing attempts targeting online-store, payment-system, and banking users rose sharply during the first ten months of the year. Its products blocked 19,063,077 attempts to access such phishing links, a 198.1% increase from the comparable 2025 period. Amazon was the most frequently impersonated brand, followed by Apple, Netflix, Shopify, and Alibaba Group-associated brands; together, these five accounted for 83.83% of phishing detections involving online stores and subscription services. Kaspersky also detected 220,071 sales-themed spam messages during the first two weeks of November, up 50.18% year over year.

The campaigns used fake login pages, payment forms, support alerts, giveaway pages, and unusually cheap offers to obtain account credentials, payment-card details, personal data, or money. Examples included fraudulent Apple support pages that push victims to call fake support numbers, fake Netflix and other streaming subscription deals, counterfeit gaming offers tied to GTA VI, and beauty or wellness scams using fake endorsements and scarcity tactics. Between June and November, Kaspersky detected 27,416 malware or potentially unwanted-application attacks disguised as GTA VI-related content. Banking Trojans remained active, with 801,150 detected attacks in the first ten months of 2026, although PC banking-malware activity declined as attackers shifted toward mobile-focused fraud and credential theft.

  • Scammers do not rely only on fake storefronts: some Apple-themed pages use alarming pop-ups and a fraudulent support number to pressure victims into disclosing sensitive information or allowing remote access to their devices.
  • Subscription promotions are a particularly effective lure because Black Friday generated an estimated 8.9 million incremental premium streaming sign-ups in 2025, giving fraudulent Netflix, Spotify, and YouTube Premium offers a believable context.
  • Gaming scams around GTA VI combine seasonal discount-seeking behavior with the game’s November 19 launch, including fake PlayStation bundles, counterfeit Steam gift-card giveaways, and Discord prompts that download suspicious files.
  • Beauty and wellness scams use fabricated medical authority, celebrity endorsements, fake customer comments, scarcity warnings, and countdown timers to make dubious products or nonexistent offers appear credible.
  • Although PC banking-malware detections declined year over year, the article notes that attackers are shifting toward mobile-focused fraud and credential theft rather than abandoning financial theft.

In plain words

The article explains how organizations can make the small software packages used to run applications safer by removing unneeded tools and locking down their settings. U.S. government rules for cloud services require these packages to meet strict safety checklists, use approved encryption where needed, and be checked regularly before being used. These steps also matter for companies outside government because they limit what an intruder can do and provide evidence that software is being managed safely.

Summary
Hardened container images remove unnecessary components and enforce secure configurations against measurable baselines such as DISA STIGs, while FIPS separately ensures approved cryptography. These practices reduce attack surface for any organization and are required in FedRAMP environments alongside continuous scanning, inventory, and pipeline enforcement.

A hardened container image removes software an application does not need, such as shells, package managers, and compilers, while enforcing restrictive settings such as non-root execution and read-only file systems. The article distinguishes hardening from minimal, distroless, and scratch images: those approaches can reduce the number of components, but do not alone prove that configuration is secure. It argues that these measures reduce an attacker’s options after access and can help organizations answer customer security questionnaires.

DISA STIGs provide U.S. Department of Defense configuration baselines with individual checks, severity levels, test instructions, and remediation guidance, while FIPS 140 separately concerns use of validated cryptographic modules in approved mode. FedRAMP requires container images to be hardened against a benchmark in NIST’s National Checklist Program and requires automated enforcement, pre-deployment scanning, registry monitoring, and asset inventory. The article emphasizes that images need continuous rebuilding and scanning as new vulnerabilities emerge, and that secure images can still be undermined by unsafe runtime choices such as deploying them as privileged Kubernetes pods.

  • A scratch image may have the smallest footprint, but it can create operational and security maintenance issues because trusted certificate authorities, user databases, and debugging tools may need to be added and maintained manually.
  • Many STIG checks for kernel settings, bootloaders, audit logging, and SSH do not apply inside containers because those functions are inherited from the host, so teams should document these as not applicable rather than ignore them.
  • A container image using FIPS-validated cryptography can still fail an assessment if its host is not operating in FIPS mode, which the article identifies as a common assessor finding.
  • Hardening can be undone at deployment time: running a hardened image as a privileged Kubernetes pod can restore the capabilities that image hardening removed.
  • Pinning an image to a digest improves reproducibility but also prevents patches from arriving automatically, since teams must deliberately move to a newly patched digest.
Key Points
  • 01A hardened container image removes software the application does not need, such as shells, package managers, and compilers, and enforces secure settings including non-root execution and read-only file systems.
  • 02DISA STIGs are U.S. Department of Defense configuration standards containing individual checks, severity levels, testing instructions, and remediation guidance for technologies including operating systems and applications.
  • 03FIPS 140 concerns validated cryptographic modules rather than image hardening, and an image must use a validated module in approved mode for all cryptographic operations to be considered FIPS-capable.
  • 04FedRAMP requires containers to be built from images hardened against a benchmark in NIST’s National Checklist Program, with automated pipeline enforcement and images scanned within the prior 30 days before running in production.
  • 05Minimal, distroless, and scratch images can reduce attack surface, but they do not by themselves prove that the image meets a secure configuration baseline.

Businesses, employees, and customers could be affected, especially where delays or downtime can cost significant money, so companies should choose security and networking designs that work reliably worldwide and continuously check AI activity.

Summary
AI and autonomous agents dramatically increase traffic, operational dependency, and security risks, but SASE’s core distributed, edge-delivered zero-trust architecture remains the right foundation. Organizations should prioritize globally distributed, single-pass SASE implementations with continuous, context-aware inspection rather than treating SASE as a checklist of features.

The article argues that AI does not require a replacement for secure access service edge (SASE), but instead represents an incremental evolution the author calls “SASE 1.2.” AI agents, alongside human users, will generate large volumes of globally distributed traffic and increasingly perform critical business functions. As a result, outages, slowdowns, and poorly controlled agent behavior can have material business consequences.

The author warns that autonomous and coordinated agents can create risks including data leaks, proprietary-model theft, compliance violations, cost overruns, and malicious code or threats. SASE should provide least-privilege access, continuous context- and behavior-based monitoring, and detailed inspection of API and JSON transactions to determine what an agent is doing. It should also be primarily cloud delivered and globally distributed, while retaining on-premises controls where desktop-based agents and local tools cannot be observed by cloud services.

The article emphasizes edge-based, single-pass routing to support data sovereignty and consistent performance for AI services. It says organizations may need to prevent agents from interacting across prohibited sovereign regions, and that even network transit through such regions can pose unacceptable risk. The author concludes that organizations should evaluate the underlying SASE architecture rather than choosing platforms based only on feature lists, because centralized or on-premises-heavy implementations may become limiting as AI use expands.

  • The article highlights that some AI agents will run directly on desktops and use local tools, meaning cloud-delivered security services may not observe all relevant activity and on-premises controls may still be necessary.
  • The author argues that data sovereignty can require preventing agents from interacting with other agents outside a permitted region, and that even routing traffic through prohibited areas can be unacceptable.
  • The article presents milliseconds of AI application performance as potentially commercially decisive, using competing pharmaceutical companies filing for a drug patent as an example.

  • 04The article recommends least-privilege access with continuous context- and behavior-based monitoring of agents, including detailed inspection of API and JSON transactions.

windows-11
Windows 11 is Microsoft’s modern desktop operating system.
WindowsUpdate.msi malware
A malicious Windows installer file made to look like a legitimate Windows update.
WinRM protocol
WinRM is a Windows remote management protocol that administrators, and sometimes attackers, use to run commands on other computers.
WinUI 3 product
WinUI 3 is a Microsoft user-interface framework for building Windows applications.
also: WinUI3
Wiz organization
A cloud security company that helps organizations identify and remediate risks in their cloud environments.
workaround concept
A workaround is a temporary way to avoid or reduce a problem without fully fixing its root cause.
workloads concept
Workloads are applications, services, or computing tasks running on servers, cloud systems, or devices.
WorkPlace product
A login portal product referenced in security reporting.
workstation product
A workstation is a computer used by a person for work, often connected to an organization's systems.
workstations product
Workstations are computers used by employees or professionals to do their daily work.
YouTube Premium product
YouTube Premium is Google’s paid YouTube subscription service offering ad-free viewing and other features.
zero data retention concept
Zero data retention is a promise or setting where a service does not store submitted data after processing it.
Zero Data Retention (ZDR) concept
Zero data retention is a policy or setting intended to prevent a service from storing customer requests and responses.
Zero trust concept
Zero trust is a security approach that does not automatically trust any user, device, or system and instead checks access continuously.
Zero Trust network access concept
A security model that requires verification for every access request, treating no user or device as trusted by default.
also: ZTNA
zero-day
A zero-day is a software flaw that attackers can exploit before the vendor has released a fix.
also: previously unknown vulnerability, previously unknown flaw
Zero-day exploitation technique
Zero-day exploitation is when attackers use a software flaw before the vendor has released a fix for it.
zero-day flaws vulnerability
Zero-day flaws are software vulnerabilities that are unknown to the vendor or have no patch available when attackers can use them.
zero-trust architecture concept
Zero-trust architecture is a security model that treats every user and device as untrusted until continuously verified.
Zscaler organization
A cybersecurity company that provides secure web gateways, zero-trust access, and cloud-delivered security services.
